title: AI detection isn't about style, it's about whether the information is watered down
dek: The tell for AI writing isn't style, it's the "information inflation" of output exceeding input. A hedge-fund titan's AI op-ed openly owning up became the turning point — Pangram's fourth generation has a false-positive rate of about 1 in 24,000, and the more models converge, the easier they are to catch.
why: The CEO personally breaks down classifier mechanics, how training data is built, the false-positive rate methodology, and casually exposes a class of online "false-accusation complaints" as astroturf. For decision-makers judging whether writing is AI, the information density is high.
who: Product and engineering leads doing content moderation, hiring screening, and education anti-cheating, plus content teams producing large volumes of text with LLMs who need to know where the line is.
skip: The Shell Game podcast and philosophical rambling at 53:00-57:00 can be skipped without losing the main thread.

points.h: "Did you use AI" is the wrong question; ask where the ideas came from
points.body: The event: Stanley Druckenmiller published an op-ed in the WSJ that any discerning reader could see was AI-written, and someone dropped it into Pangram and got a 100% AI verdict. The turning point was that he didn't hide it — he directly admitted "I'm fundamentally not a good writer, I just used AI" — and the WSJ refused to retract. Bryan pushed one step further: since he's owning up, show the prompt. "Did you use AI" is a false binary; the real question is where the ideas came from — was it "write me an op-ed against the Treasury's action," or "here are my five pages of notes, polish them into an article."

points.h: Detecting AI is theoretically impossible, practically good enough
points.body: In 2023 Max asked research friends whether AI text could be detected, and the answer was unanimous: "impossible, don't try, and the models will only get stronger." Pangram's response was to abandon theoretical counterexamples ("just have ChatGPT paraphrase any text and you've disproven it") and care only about the practical case: when the information content of the input is less than the output, that's the trace of AI involvement, which Bryan calls word inflation. This definition also explains why early Yelp/Amazon fake reviews never became a breakthrough — platforms figured AI reviews were only 3% of the total, not painful enough to matter.

points.h: Catching AI isn't about em dashes, it's about synthetic mirroring
points.body: Pangram is a classifier model, not a surface-rule em dash detector. The approach: cut off an open-source LLM's "predict the next word" head and replace it with a classification head that outputs a 0-15 AI-involvement score. Training data is built with "synthetic mirroring": take a human-written article and have an LLM compress it into a prompt ("write 200 words covering these three points"), then feed that to a random frontier model, yielding a paired sample of a human version and an AI version on the same topic. The second layer is editing prompts, then clause-level labeling: text left as-is is human, text that was changed is AI-assisted, and new sentences conjured from nothing are AI-generated.

points.h: A detector's lifeline is its false-positive rate, not its accuracy
points.body: Pangram 4's false-positive rate is about 1/24,000, measured by running millions of pre-2022 documents (an era when AI ghostwriting was nearly impossible); the false-negative rate is about 1/300, measured by taking real user prompts from WildChat and regenerating them with frontier models. Not perfect, but the direction is right. Bryan's experience is that false positives are extremely low, and that is precisely the lifeline for whether a product can be taken seriously. Pangram 4's step change came from switching from a 512-token window to token-level output: an entirely human-written document with two AI sentences stuck in the middle can be pointed out word by word.

points.h: A detector doesn't need to be 100%, it just needs to make cheating costly
points.body: Max says education is a huge market, and this year is the first time anyone has realized "there exist genuinely usable AI detectors." The product logic isn't 100% precision but creating friction on the shortcut — turning "throw the assignment at AI" from zero-cost into costly, so students take the next-easiest path, which is doing it themselves. The same judgment applies to enterprise settings: Oxide's hiring is a writing-intensive process, and an LLM-parroted "why I want to join Oxide" written in corporate boilerplate is recognizable at a glance; the detector just makes it explicit.

points.h: Most "I was falsely flagged" sob stories are astroturf ads
points.body: Max distinguishes two kinds of opposition. One group genuinely wishes detectors didn't exist: it lets AI text produced in their profession be authoritatively identified. The other is marketing from the humanizer ecosystem: these tools claim to rewrite AI text so it fools Turnitin and Pangram, sold to students caught cheating on assignments; they usually also bundle an "AI detector" that first declares your text AI, then sells you the rewriting service. Many of the Reddit sob stories about "my teacher falsely flagged me at 76% AI and gave me a zero" are this kind of lead-gen astroturf — drop them into Pangram and they're all AI-written.

points.h: Stronger models haven't made detection harder, but easier
points.body: Asked whether he's forever chasing the frontier model, Max gives a counterintuitive judgment: two things happen at once — models get smarter, but after post-training repeatedly teaches "correctness" and preferences, the output distribution is far narrower than in the GPT-2 era. GPT-2 tried to simulate the full human output distribution; today's models only give "correct" tokens, not what an ordinary person would say. He and the three Oxide people share the same feel: new models talk with a "strangely erudite" flavor, and detection hasn't gotten harder, it's gotten easier to pick up.

points.h: The next argument is how much the human actually input
points.body: Pangram can already guess the model family internally: the probe's top-1 accuracy is 90%, but to productize it would need to reach 98%. The further direction is "reverse Pangram" — inferring what prompt might have generated this text and how much context the model was given: two bullet points or fifteen? The information content of this dimension completely changes the characterization of Druckenmiller's op-ed — giving five pages of notes to polish counts as collaboration, giving five bullet points to expand is ghostwriting. The next argument in detection isn't "was AI used," it's "how much did the human actually input."
